gloss_terse: going in, setting (of the sun); sunset
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears only in Daniel 6:14, where it describes the time when the sun goes down. The Aramaic word derives from a root meaning 'to enter' or 'go in,' and in this context refers to the sun's entrance into the western horizon. The phrase 'at the setting of the sun' marks the urgent deadline by which the king's sealed decree could not be reversed, even to save Daniel.

senses.1: The multilingual evidence shows translators recognizing this as a temporal marker tied to sunset: English 'setting-of,' Spanish 'la-puesta-de' (the setting of), and French 'de-sur-moi' suggest the sun's descent. This Aramaic term uses the concept of the sun 'entering' or 'going into' the west to mark the close of day (Dan 6:14).

gloss_terse: lifting, raising up; the act of lifting hands in worship
gloss_readable: Found only in Nehemiah 8:6, this noun describes the physical action of the people lifting their hands in response to Ezra's blessing. The word comes from the root meaning 'to go up' or 'ascend.' In ancient Near Eastern worship, raising hands was a standard posture of prayer, surrender, and receiving blessing. Here the lifting of hands accompanies vocal worship and physical prostration.

senses.1: Translators across languages capture the action of raising: English 'with-lifting-of,' Spanish 'con-alzar' (with raising). The context in Nehemiah shows the people's hands going upward in a gesture of worship and affirmation after hearing God's word read and explained. This upward motion expresses both reverence and reception.

gloss_terse: what rises up; thoughts, plans (metaphorical)
gloss_readable: Occurring only in Ezekiel 11:5, this feminine plural noun literally means 'things that come up' or 'ascents.' The prophet uses it metaphorically for the thoughts or plans that arise in people's minds—the mental formations that 'come up' in consciousness. God declares that He knows 'the things that come up in your spirit,' i.e., your inmost thoughts and schemes, whether righteous or wicked.

senses.1: The multilingual glosses reveal interpretive diversity: English 'what-rises-of' preserves the upward movement metaphor, Spanish 'subidas-de' (risings of) likewise, while German 'Stufen' (steps/stairs) and French 'degré' (step/degree) show the concrete architectural sense bleeding into the translation. The image is of thoughts ascending into awareness, known fully to God (Ezek 11:5).

gloss_terse: standing ground, foothold; a firm place to stand
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in Psalm 69:2, where the psalmist cries out, 'I have come into deep waters, and there is no foothold.' The word denotes a solid place where one's feet can grip and stand securely. In the psalm's drowning metaphor, the absence of foothold intensifies the sense of helplessness and peril—sinking into mire with nothing firm beneath.

senses.1: The English and German glosses both use 'foothold,' capturing the idea of a secure standing place. Spanish expands to 'donde-estar-en-pie' (where to stand upright), and French 'de-se-tenir' (to hold oneself) reflects the need for stability. The psalmist's imagery draws on the terror of quicksand or deep water where no solid ground can be found (Ps 69:2).

gloss_terse: burden, heavy stone; something difficult to lift or bear
gloss_readable: Found only in Zechariah 12:3, this word describes Jerusalem as 'a burdensome stone' for all peoples—a stone so heavy that those who try to lift it will be severely injured. The imagery draws on the challenge of moving massive building stones or the sport of stone-lifting. What appears liftable proves crushing to those who attempt it, symbolizing the futility of opposing God's chosen city.

senses.1: English and French both use 'burden/fardeau,' while Spanish chooses 'pesada' (heavy [stone]). The image in Zechariah is of a stone that invites lifting but exceeds the lifter's capacity, resulting in injury. This 'burden-stone' becomes a metaphor for Jerusalem's supernatural resilience against her enemies.

gloss_terse: Maats; a personal name in Judah's genealogy
gloss_readable: This proper name appears once in 1 Chronicles 2:27 as a son in Judah's lineage through Jerahmeel. The name's etymology is uncertain, though it may relate to roots involving anger or counsel. The Septuagint renders it as 'Maas.' Such genealogical records preserve clan memory and tribal identity within Israel's complex family structure.

senses.1: Translators typically transliterate personal names with minor variations: English 'Ma'ats,' Spanish 'Maats.' The name appears in the extended genealogy that traces secondary lines within Judah, situating this individual within Israel's tribal memory (1 Chr 2:27).

gloss_terse: place of pain, torment; where suffering is experienced
gloss_readable: This noun occurs only in Isaiah 50:11, where God warns those who kindle their own fires that they will 'lie down in torment.' The word can mean either a place characterized by pain or pain itself. The prophetic context suggests a place of suffering as the consequence of self-reliance and rebellion. Those who light their own way rather than trusting God's servant end in anguish.

senses.1: English 'in-torment' and Spanish 'en-dolor' (in pain) both capture the idea of entering or lying down in a state or place of suffering. The preposition 'to/in' suggests both destination and condition—the rebels will end up in a place defined by pain, the fruit of their own fire-kindling (Isa 50:11).

gloss_terse: restraint, hindrance; obstacle preventing action
gloss_readable: Appearing only in 1 Samuel 14:6, this word expresses Jonathan's faith that 'the LORD has no restraint in delivering, whether by many or by few.' The noun denotes something that hinders or holds back action. Jonathan's declaration affirms that God faces no obstacle, no limiting factor in His power to save—numerical disadvantage means nothing to omnipotence.

senses.1: English, French, and German all use 'restraint,' while Spanish offers 'impedimento' (impediment). Jonathan's bold assertion before attacking the Philistine garrison rests on the theological principle that God's saving power operates independently of human military strength or numbers (1 Sam 14:6).

gloss_terse: restraint, self-control; governance over one's spirit
gloss_readable: This word appears only in Proverbs 25:28, comparing a person without self-control to 'a city broken down, without walls.' The noun denotes the capacity to restrain or govern one's impulses, particularly one's spirit or temper. Just as walls protect a city from invasion, self-control protects a person from destructive passions. The absence of this restraint leaves one defenseless and vulnerable.

senses.1: English 'restraint' and Spanish 'dominio' (mastery/control) capture the governing function. The Proverbs image likens internal discipline to civic fortification: without walls, a city falls to any invader; without self-governance, a person falls to every impulse (Prov 25:28).

gloss_terse: parapet, railing; protective barrier on a roof or height
gloss_readable: Found only in Deuteronomy 22:8, this word designates the protective railing required on the edge of a flat roof. Ancient Israelite homes had flat roofs used for various activities, creating a danger of falls. The law mandates a parapet to prevent bloodguilt if someone should fall. This reflects Israel's ethical concern for the safety of others and accountability for preventable harm.

senses.1: English, French, and German all transliterate or translate as 'parapet,' while Spanish uses 'barandilla' (railing). The Torah's requirement shows practical love of neighbor expressed in building codes—a parapet makes the roof safe for visitors and family members (Deut 22:8).

gloss_terse: crooked places, twisted paths; morally or physically bent things
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears once in Isaiah 42:16, where God promises to make 'crooked places straight' for His people. The word denotes things twisted, bent, or perverse—the opposite of straight or level. In prophetic literature, this often carries moral connotations of injustice or corruption, though here it may describe difficult terrain. God's redemptive work includes straightening what is bent and making rough places smooth.

senses.1: Spanish 'lo-torcido' (the twisted) and English 'crooked-places' both preserve the sense of deviation from straightness. The prophet contrasts these with 'level ground,' describing God's transformative guidance that removes obstacles and corrects distortions for those who follow Him (Isa 42:16).

gloss_terse: bare place, open space; exposed ground or clear area
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears in Judges 20:33 in a difficult textual context, apparently referring to an open or exposed area near Gibeah. The word derives from a root meaning 'to be bare or naked,' suggesting a clear, unobstructed space—perhaps a field or plaza where troops could deploy. Some versions understand it as a place name (Maareh-geba), while others see it as describing the tactical ground.

senses.1: English 'from-Maareh' and Spanish 'desde-prado-de' (from meadow of) reflect the interpretive difficulty—is this a toponym or a description? French and German treat it as a place name. The military context in Judges suggests Israelite troops emerging from an open area to engage Benjamin's forces (Judg 20:33).

gloss_terse: Mearah; a cave or cave-town in northern Canaan
gloss_readable: This proper noun appears only in Joshua 13:4 in a list of unconquered territories. The name means 'cave' and may refer to a specific cave-town or region characterized by caves near Sidon in Phoenician territory. The Israelites did not fully occupy this northern area, which remained under Canaanite control. The name itself reflects the prominence of cave dwellings in the region's geography.

senses.1: Translators handle this as a proper name with slight variations: English 'Mearah,' Spanish 'Meará,' French and German preserve the transliteration. The geographical reference marks the northern boundary of Israel's incomplete conquest, a cave-region that remained outside their control (Josh 13:4).

gloss_terse: plans, arrangements; ordered thoughts or preparations of the mind
gloss_readable: Found only in Proverbs 16:1, this plural noun denotes the arrangements, plans, or ordered thoughts that a person devises. The proverb states, 'To man belong the plans of the heart, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD.' This sets up a contrast between human initiative in planning and divine sovereignty in outcomes. We make our mental arrangements, but God determines what actually gets spoken and accomplished.

senses.1: English 'plans-of' and Spanish 'planes-de' both capture the sense of deliberate mental ordering. The 'plans of the heart' are the internal preparations and schemes people devise, yet the proverb reminds us that execution and fruition depend on God's will, not merely human intention (Prov 16:1).

gloss_terse: naked ones, those without clothing; people in a state of exposure
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in 2 Chronicles 28:15, describing Israelite captives who had been stripped by their captors. The word emphasizes their vulnerable, exposed condition—lacking basic clothing and dignity. Compassionate leaders from the northern kingdom clothed these 'naked ones,' gave them food and drink, anointed their wounds, and returned them to their families. This rare act of mercy across tribal divisions stands out in Israel's civil conflicts.

senses.1: English 'their-naked-ones' and Spanish 'desnudos-de-ellos' (naked ones of them) both preserve the focus on people deprived of clothing. The narrative shows these exposed captives receiving merciful treatment—clothed, fed, and restored—reversing their shameful condition (2 Chr 28:15).

gloss_terse: terror, awful crash; violent shock or destruction
gloss_readable: This noun occurs only in Isaiah 10:33, where it describes the terrifying crash as the LORD lops off the tree-crown of Assyria's pride. The word conveys both the sound and the impact of violent destruction—an awful shock that accompanies divine judgment. The metaphor pictures Assyria as a towering forest that God will cut down with terrifying force, reducing the proud empire to stumps.

senses.1: English 'with-terror' and Spanish 'con-terror' both emphasize the fearful aspect of this violent act. The context describes God wielding judgment like an axe, and the crash of falling trees symbolizes the shock and awe of Assyria's sudden collapse under divine wrath (Isa 10:33).

gloss_terse: Maarath; a town in the hill country of Judah
gloss_readable: This place name appears once in Joshua 15:59 in the list of Judahite towns. The name may derive from the root for 'cave,' suggesting a settlement near caves or in cave-riddled terrain. The exact location is uncertain, though it belonged to the hill country district of Judah. The Septuagint renders it as 'Maarath' or 'Maroth.' Such town lists preserve the territorial allotments of Israel's tribes.

senses.1: English 'Maarath,' Spanish 'Maarat,' and French/German preserve the transliteration with slight variation. The town name appears in the extended list of Judah's inheritance, marking one settlement among many in the central highlands (Josh 15:59).

gloss_terse: Maasai; a priestly name, variant of Maaseiah
gloss_readable: This personal name occurs once in 1 Chronicles 9:12, identifying a priest in post-exilic Jerusalem. It appears to be a shortened form of Maaseiah, which means 'work of the LORD.' The genealogical list in Chronicles traces priestly families who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, establishing continuity with pre-exilic worship. Such names testify to families' identity and divine calling.

senses.1: English 'Maasai' and Spanish 'Maasai' both transliterate the name consistently. The priestly genealogy establishes this individual's lineage and role in the restored temple service, linking post-exilic worship to Israel's ancestral priestly orders (1 Chr 9:12).

gloss_terse: Memphis; the ancient capital of Lower Egypt
gloss_readable: This place name refers to the great Egyptian city Memphis (Egyptian Men-nefer), which served as Egypt's capital for much of its history. Located south of the Nile Delta, Memphis was a center of power, culture, and idolatry. The prophets pronounce judgment on this proud city, predicting its downfall and desolation. Hosea 9:6 mentions Memphis as a place where Israelites would be buried in exile—an ironic reversal of Egypt's monumental burial culture.

senses.1: English 'Memphis,' Spanish 'Menfis,' and French 'Memphis' all identify the famous Egyptian capital. The prophetic references consistently portray Memphis as representing Egypt's pride and power, destined for divine humiliation. Israel's association with Memphis in exile represents national disgrace (Hos 9:6).

gloss_terse: target, mark; object of aim or attack
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in Job 7:20, where Job asks God, 'Why have you made me your target?' The word denotes something aimed at, a mark for arrows or assault. Job feels singled out for divine attack, as if God has set him up as a target for affliction. This captures Job's anguished sense of being specifically chosen for suffering, unable to understand why God would focus hostile attention on a mortal.

senses.1: English 'as-target' and Spanish 'como-blanco' (as target/bull's-eye) both preserve the archery metaphor. Job's rhetorical question expresses his bewilderment at becoming the object of God's apparent hostility, as though set up for divine target practice (Job 7:20).

gloss_terse: breathing out, expiring; the final breath of life
gloss_readable: This noun occurs only in Job 11:20, where Zophar warns the wicked that 'the expiring of life will be their hope'—meaning death is all they can look forward to. The word literally denotes the breathing out or exhaling of the life-breath, the moment when breath departs and life ends. In ancient physiology, breath was synonymous with life itself, so its final exhalation marked the transition to death.

senses.1: Spanish 'será-el-último-suspiro-del' (will be the last sigh of) beautifully captures the dying breath imagery. The phrase 'breathing out of life' describes expiration in both senses—breathing out and dying. Zophar uses this to depict the hopelessness awaiting the wicked (Job 11:20).

gloss_terse: bellows; instrument for blowing air to intensify fire
gloss_readable: This word appears only in Jeremiah 6:29, in a metallurgical metaphor for failed prophetic ministry. The prophet pictures himself as a refiner trying to purify Israel, but 'the bellows blow fiercely, the lead is consumed by the fire'—yet the refining fails because the wicked are not removed. Bellows were essential for achieving the high temperatures needed to smelt and refine metal. Their fierce blowing represents prophetic intensity that nonetheless fails to purify a rebellious people.

senses.1: English and Spanish both use 'bellows/el-fuelle,' the standard term for the air-blowing device. Jeremiah's metaphor draws on the refining process: despite maximum heat (fierce bellows), the ore refuses to yield pure metal because the impurities are too deeply embedded—Israel's wickedness resists even intense prophetic fire (Jer 6:29).

gloss_terse: Muppim; a son of Benjamin, clan founder
gloss_readable: This personal name appears only in Genesis 46:21 as one of Benjamin's sons who went down to Egypt with Jacob's family. The name's meaning is uncertain. In 1 Chronicles 7:12, a variant 'Shuppim' appears in Benjamin's genealogy, suggesting textual fluidity in these clan names. Such variations may reflect different clan traditions or scribal updating of archaic forms.

senses.1: English 'Muppim,' Spanish 'Mupim,' French and German 'Muppim' all transliterate the name with minor variation. The Genesis genealogy includes this figure among the seventy who entered Egypt, establishing his role as an ancestral clan head within Benjamin's tribe (Gen 46:21).

gloss_terse: club, war hammer; shattering weapon
gloss_readable: This noun appears twice with uncertain meaning—in Nahum 2:2 and Proverbs 25:18. Modern scholars often emend it to 'club' or 'hammer,' understanding it as a weapon that shatters or scatters. Proverbs compares a false witness to 'a club, a sword, and a sharp arrow'—instruments of violence and harm. The image conveys how destructive dishonest testimony can be, crushing innocent people like a war hammer.

senses.1: English 'a-club' and Spanish 'Maza' (mace/club) both understand the term as a blunt weapon. The Proverbs context groups it with other weapons to illustrate the violent damage caused by false witness—like being struck with a hammer, run through with a sword, or pierced with an arrow (Prov 25:18).

gloss_terse: wonders, marvelous works; acts of extraordinary character
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in Job 37:16 in a textually uncertain passage, apparently referring to God's wondrous works in nature, particularly cloud formations. The word derives from a root meaning 'to be extraordinary or difficult.' Elihu is calling Job's attention to the marvels of God's providential control over weather—the 'wonders' of the one perfect in knowledge. Some scholars emend the text, but the sense of divine marvels fits the context well.

senses.1: English 'the-wonders-of' and Spanish 'maravillas-de' (marvels of) both capture the sense of extraordinary phenomena. Elihu's speech emphasizes God's wisdom displayed in meteorological wonders—clouds, lightning, storms—that demonstrate knowledge and power far beyond human comprehension (Job 37:16).

gloss_terse: divisions, courses; organizational groups or classes
gloss_readable: This plural noun occurs only in 2 Chronicles 35:12, describing how the Passover offerings were distributed 'according to the divisions of the fathers' houses.' The word denotes organizational groupings or courses, likely referring to the divisions by which families or clans received their portions of the sacrifices. This reflects the orderly administration of worship under Josiah's reform, ensuring proper distribution according to tribal and family structure.

senses.1: English 'to-divisions-of' and Spanish 'a-divisiones-de' (to divisions of) both preserve the sense of organized groupings. The Chronicler's account emphasizes the careful ordering of Josiah's Passover, with offerings distributed systematically to family divisions rather than in chaos (2 Chr 35:12).

gloss_terse: ruin, heap of ruins; destroyed city reduced to rubble
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in Isaiah 17:1, in the oracle against Damascus: 'Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins.' The word denotes the state of complete destruction, a city reduced to a pile of rubble. This prophetic judgment envisions the proud Syrian capital demolished and abandoned, transformed from thriving metropolis to desolate ruin-heap.

senses.1: English and Spanish both use 'ruins/ruinas,' the standard term for destroyed buildings. Isaiah's oracle depicts Damascus's utter devastation—no longer functioning as a city but collapsed into a mere mound of stones, a monument to divine judgment (Isa 17:1).

gloss_terse: escape, place of escape; deliverance or refuge from danger
gloss_readable: This word occurs only in Psalm 55:8, where the psalmist longs to 'hasten to my escape from the raging wind and tempest.' The noun can mean either the act of escaping or a place of escape. The context suggests flight from overwhelming danger, seeking a safe haven away from conspiracies and violence. Some interpret it as 'deliverer' rather than 'escape,' but the sense of refuge from storm imagery fits the parallel structure well.

senses.1: English 'my-escape' and Spanish 'escape' both emphasize the idea of getting away or finding refuge. The psalmist yearns to flee like a dove to wilderness safety, away from the social and political storms threatening to destroy him (Ps 55:8).

gloss_terse: balancings, spreadings; the hovering or suspending of clouds
gloss_readable: This rare noun appears only in Job 37:16, in Elihu's speech about God's wisdom displayed in weather phenomena. The word apparently describes the spreading out or balancing of clouds in the sky—how they hang suspended and spread across the heavens. This may refer to the visual wonder of cloud formations or the physics of how clouds float and spread. Some scholars emend to 'spreadings' to match 36:29, but the image of balanced suspension fits the context of divine marvels.

senses.1: English 'the-balancings-of' and Spanish 'balanceos-de' (balancings of) both preserve the sense of suspension or equilibrium. Elihu marvels at how clouds are poised and spread in the sky, a phenomenon demonstrating the perfect knowledge of the God who governs atmospheric physics (Job 37:16).

gloss_terse: works, things made; creative productions or accomplishments
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in Proverbs 8:22, where Wisdom personified declares, 'The LORD possessed me at the beginning of his way, before his works of old.' The word denotes things made or produced, creative works or accomplishments. In this context, it refers to God's ancient creative acts—Wisdom existed before any of the cosmos came into being. This establishes Wisdom's primordial status and intimate role in creation.

senses.1: English 'His-works' and Spanish 'obras-de-él' (works of him) both capture the sense of divine creative products. Wisdom's self-testimony places her before all of God's making, prior even to the first acts of creation—she precedes and participates in all God's works (Prov 8:22).

gloss_terse: shattering weapon, instrument of destruction; tool for breaking
gloss_readable: This noun occurs only in Ezekiel 9:2, describing the six executioners who come with 'weapons of destruction in their hands.' The word denotes an implement designed to shatter or smash—a club, axe, or other lethal tool. These figures represent divine agents of judgment who will execute God's wrath on Jerusalem's idolaters. The 'shattering weapon' symbolizes the violence and thoroughness of the coming destruction.

senses.1: English 'shattering-of-him' preserves the breaking/smashing aspect, while Spanish 'destrucción-de-él' (destruction of him) and French 'massacre' emphasize the lethal outcome. Ezekiel's vision portrays these angelic executioners carrying implements designed to kill, executing divine judgment on the city's guilty inhabitants (Ezek 9:2).

gloss_terse: war club, shattering weapon; instrument used in battle to break enemies
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in Jeremiah 51:20, where God addresses Babylon: 'You are my war club, my weapon of battle; with you I shatter nations.' The word denotes a heavy club or hammer used to crush and shatter. God ironically identifies Babylon as His instrument for executing judgment on other nations—the very empire that will itself be shattered. The imagery conveys both power and violence, the blunt-force crushing of military conquest.

senses.1: English 'a-war-club' and Spanish 'martillo' (hammer) both capture the heavy shattering weapon. Jeremiah's oracle reveals the paradox of Babylon's role: chosen as God's club to break nations, yet destined to be broken in turn when its usefulness ends (Jer 51:20).

gloss_terse: Muster Gate; gate in Jerusalem's wall, possibly for military assembly
gloss_readable: This term appears only in Nehemiah 3:31, referring to 'the Muster Gate' in Jerusalem's wall. The name suggests a gate associated with military muster or appointed assembly—possibly where troops gathered for inspection or deployment. The exact location is uncertain, though it was part of the wall circuit that Nehemiah's teams rebuilt. Such named gates served both functional and symbolic roles in ancient cities.

senses.1: English 'the-Muster' and Spanish 'la-inspección' (the inspection) both reflect the military/administrative function. The gate name likely commemorates its role as a gathering point for census-taking, troop formation, or official appointments—a place where order and readiness were established (Neh 3:31).

gloss_terse: landings, harbors; coastal places where ships dock
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in Judges 5:17, in Deborah's victory song, where she asks, 'Why did Dan remain with the ships? Asher sat still at his landings.' The word apparently refers to harbors, docks, or landing places along the coast where ships come to shore. The Song criticizes these coastal tribes for staying safely at their ports rather than joining the battle against Sisera—commercial interests trumped covenant obligation.

senses.1: English 'his-landings' and Spanish 'sus-puertos' (his ports) both identify maritime facilities. The poetic rebuke highlights Dan and Asher's comfortable coastal position—they remained at their secure harbors engaged in shipping rather than risking themselves in inland warfare (Judg 5:17).

gloss_terse: neck; part of body connecting head to torso, especially the back of the neck
gloss_readable: This noun occurs only in 1 Samuel 4:18, describing how Eli 'fell backward from his seat beside the gate, and his neck was broken and he died.' The word specifically denotes the neck as the dividing point between head and body. The elderly priest's fatal fall upon hearing of the ark's capture represents the shattering of Israel's spiritual leadership. The broken neck symbolizes the broken covenant relationship.

senses.1: English 'his-neck' and Spanish 'su-cerviz' (his neck/nape) both identify the body part that fractured in Eli's fall. The neck-breaking represents both literal cause of death and symbolic judgment—the heavy, aged priest cannot bear the weight of Israel's disaster (1 Sam 4:18).

gloss_terse: buttocks, hips; lower stepping region of the body
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in 1 Chronicles 19:4, parallel to 2 Samuel 10:4, where Hanun humiliates David's ambassadors by cutting their garments 'up to the buttocks.' The word denotes the hip or buttock region, the 'stepping region' of the body. Exposing this area was a severe public shaming in ancient Near Eastern culture, turning a diplomatic mission into an insult that provoked war. The deliberate exposure of the buttocks violated honor and demanded response.

senses.1: English 'the-buttocks' and Spanish 'las-nalgas' (the buttocks) both identify the exposed body part. The shameful cutting of the ambassadors' robes to reveal their lower bodies constituted a deliberate diplomatic insult, treating honored envoys like prisoners of war (1 Chr 19:4).

gloss_terse: siege work, palisade; military fortification or entrenchment
gloss_readable: This word appears only in Isaiah 29:3, where God declares He will 'encamp against you all around and lay siege with a palisade.' The noun denotes some type of siege work—possibly a palisade, tower, or entrenchment used in attacking a fortified city. The parallel term 'siegeworks' confirms the military context. God ironically becomes the besieger of His own city Jerusalem, turning divine protection into divine assault due to the people's hypocrisy.

senses.1: English 'with-a-siege-work' and Spanish 'con-puesto' (with post/position) both suggest military installations. Isaiah's oracle reverses expectations—the LORD who defended Jerusalem now encircles it with siege equipment, treating His city as an enemy fortress to be reduced (Isa 29:3).

gloss_terse: the Mesobaite; gentile designation, origin uncertain
gloss_readable: This gentile designation appears only in 1 Chronicles 11:47, attached to one of David's mighty warriors. The term apparently indicates place of origin, but the location is unknown and the form is unusual. Some scholars suggest emending to 'from Zobah,' a known region, while ancient versions vary widely in their renderings. The obscurity may result from textual corruption or preservation of a now-forgotten place name.

senses.1: English 'the-Metsovayah' and Spanish 'el-metsobayá' attempt to transliterate the uncertain term. The gentile marker identifies one of David's elite warriors by hometown or region, but the exact referent remains mysterious—possibly a small village whose name survived only in this military roster (1 Chr 11:47).

gloss_terse: Mozah; a town in Benjamin's territory
gloss_readable: This place name appears only in Joshua 18:26 in the boundary list for Benjamin's tribal allotment. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to go out' or 'origin.' The exact location remains uncertain, though it belonged to Benjamin's towns in the central hill country. The Septuagint renders it variously, reflecting uncertainty even in antiquity. Such boundary lists preserve the geographical memory of Israel's tribal divisions.

senses.1: English 'ha-Motsah,' Spanish 'Mosa,' and French/German transliterations all treat this as a proper place name. The town appears in Benjamin's allocation, one of many settlements defining the boundaries of the smallest but strategically important tribe (Josh 18:26).

gloss_terse: siegeworks, fortifications; military constructions for attack or defense
gloss_readable: This plural noun appears only in Ecclesiastes 9:14, describing how 'a great king came and built great siegeworks against' a small city. The word denotes military fortifications or siege installations—towers, ramps, palisades used to assault a defended city. The Preacher's parable illustrates that wisdom, though more valuable than military might, is often unrecognized and unrewarded. The 'great siegeworks' represent overwhelming force that wisdom nevertheless overcomes.

senses.1: English 'siegeworks,' Spanish 'baluartes' (bulwarks), and French 'forteresse' (fortress) all capture military construction. Qohelet's story contrasts massive siege apparatus with the quiet wisdom of one poor man who delivers the city—yet is forgotten despite his greater power (Eccl 9:14).
